title: Theranostics for Meningioma on the Rise: New EANM/ EANO/RANO/SNMMI Guidelines Pave the Way to Improved Patient Outcomes Using Radiolabeled Somatostatin Receptor Ligands
study_design: Editorial discussing joint EANM/EANO/RANO/SNMMI guidelines for SSTR-targeted PET imaging and radiopharmaceutical therapy in meningioma; no original study methods are reported.
condition_or_topic: SSTR-targeted PET imaging and radiopharmaceutical therapy for meningiomas
clinical_background: Meningiomas are the most frequent primary intracranial tumors in adults and have variable clinical courses. Although surgery can cure most cases, 20%–25% recur and require further treatment. Most meningiomas express high levels of somatostatin receptors, particularly SSTR2, supporting interest in radiolabeled SSTR ligands for imaging and therapy. Standards for their use in routine care and trials had been unavailable; EANM, EANO, RANO, and SNMMI have recently issued joint guidance. Evidence for radiopharmaceutical therapy remains limited to small case series and small, uncontrolled prospective trials.

main_findings.description: Meningioma recurs in a proportion of cases that require further treatment.
main_findings.context: Background estimate cited by the editorial; not a result generated by this article.

main_findings.description: Most meningiomas have high somatostatin receptor expression, particularly SSTR2.
main_findings.context: Finding from previously published evidence cited by the editorial.

main_findings.description: A cited study found [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET/MRI to be cost-effective for meningioma management.
main_findings.context: The finding pertains to a U.S. health care setting; the editorial provides no numerical estimate.

main_findings.description: An interim analysis of an ongoing single-arm phase II trial reported that its predefined progression-free survival threshold was met.
main_findings.context: The threshold was assessed at 6-mo. This is a result of the cited trial, not of the editorial; the rate and threshold value are not given.

secondary_results: The cited interim analysis identified [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET as a potentially useful imaging biomarker for assessing response to radiopharmaceutical therapy; no quantitative result is provided.
interpretation: The authors consider the new EANM/EANO/RANO/SNMMI guidelines an important step toward consistent, evidence-based, and safe use of SSTR-targeted PET and radiopharmaceutical therapy for meningioma. They expect the guidelines to support broader clinical use, while emphasizing that adequately controlled evidence is still needed.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Previously, standardized guidance for these approaches was unavailable. A cited U.S. study demonstrated the cost-effectiveness of [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET/MRI for meningioma management. An interim analysis of a separate, ongoing single-arm phase II trial reported that its predefined progression-free survival threshold at 6 mo was met and suggested that [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET could help assess response to radiopharmaceutical therapy.
clinical_implications: SSTR-targeted PET is increasingly considered for differential diagnosis, defining tumor extent, planning surgery or radiotherapy, distinguishing recurrence from treatment-related changes, and estimating prognosis.
The authors expect the guidelines to improve access to SSTR-targeted PET through insurance reimbursement in the United States, with potential benefits for clinical outcomes.
practice_implications: The guidelines offer expert guidance on when to use SSTR-targeted PET, how to acquire and interpret images, and how to report findings.

For SSTR-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy, the guidelines provide procedural standards covering administration, accompanying medications, dosimetry, monitoring, adverse-effect management, and quality control.
limitations: Evidence for radiopharmaceutical therapy in meningioma currently comes only from small case series and small, uncontrolled prospective trials.
The authors state that adequately designed, controlled prospective multicenter trials are still needed to support routine neuro-oncology use of SSTR-directed PET and radiopharmaceutical therapy.
strengths: The guidelines bring together EANM, EANO, RANO, and SNMMI and provide a comprehensive reference for imaging and therapeutic procedures.
open_questions: Controlled evidence on [177Lu]Lu-DOTATATE for recurrent meningioma is not yet available.
Standardized PET-based criteria for assessing meningioma response have yet to be developed.
future_directions: The authors call for adequately designed, controlled prospective multicenter trials of SSTR-directed PET and radiopharmaceutical therapy in meningioma.
RANO plans to develop standardized PET-based response criteria for meningioma.
The first randomized trial of [177Lu]Lu-DOTATATE for recurrent meningioma, LUMEN-1; NCT06326190, is scheduled to begin enrolling patients in the first quarter of 2025.
The authors anticipate future efforts to obtain insurance reimbursement for SSTR-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy.
main_conclusion: The authors consider the new EANM/EANO/RANO/SNMMI guidelines an important step toward consistent, evidence-based, and safe use of SSTR-targeted PET imaging and radiopharmaceutical therapy for meningioma. They also emphasize that adequately designed, controlled prospective multicenter trials are needed to support wider clinical adoption.
narrative_summary:
This editorial examines the clinical role of SSTR-targeted imaging and radiopharmaceutical therapy for meningioma and the newly developed EANM/EANO/RANO/SNMMI practice guidelines. Although surgery cures most meningiomas, 20%–25% recur and require further treatment. Most meningiomas express SSTRs, particularly SSTR2, providing a basis for the use of radiolabeled SSTR ligands.

The authors describe increasing use of SSTR-targeted PET for differential diagnosis, assessment of tumor extent, surgical and radiotherapy planning, distinguishing recurrence from treatment-related changes, and prognostication. Its use for disease monitoring has also been proposed. Evidence for radiopharmaceutical therapy remains limited to small case series and small, uncontrolled prospective trials. An interim analysis of an ongoing single-arm phase II trial reported that its predefined progression-free survival rate at the 6-mo threshold was met; the analysis also identified [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET as a potentially useful biomarker of treatment response. The first randomized trial of [177Lu]Lu-DOTATATE for recurrent meningioma, LUMEN-1 (NCT06326190), was scheduled to begin enrolling patients in the first quarter of 2025.

The guidelines address PET indications, acquisition, interpretation, and reporting, alongside procedures for radiopharmaceutical therapy. The authors expect them to improve standardization and patient access while stressing the need for adequately designed, controlled prospective multicenter trials before these approaches can be effectively integrated into routine neuro-oncology practice.

document_sections.heading: Theranostics for Meningioma on the Rise: New EANM/ EANO/RANO/SNMMI Guidelines Pave the Way to Improved Patient Outcomes Using Radiolabeled Somatostatin Receptor Ligands
document_sections.content: Meningiomas are the most common primary intracranial tumors in adults, and their clinical course varies substantially. Surgery cures most cases, but 20%–25% recur and require further treatment, which may include another resection, radiotherapy, or experimental drug therapy. Most meningiomas express somatostatin receptors (SSTRs) at high levels, particularly SSTR2, making radiolabeled SSTR ligands a promising means of improving management. Until recently, routine practice and clinical trials lacked guidelines to standardize SSTR-targeted PET imaging and radiopharmaceutical therapy. EANM, SNMMI, EANO, and the RANO PET task force have now jointly issued practice guidance and procedure standards for these approaches in meningioma. The most frequently used tracers for SSTR-targeted PET are octreotide-derived, 68Ga-labeled SSTR agonist tracers, including [68Ga]Ga-DOTATOC, [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE, and [68Ga]Ga-DOTANOC. In the United States, [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE and [64Cu]Cu-DOTATATE are readily available; insurance coverage varies but is increasing overall. A cited study demonstrated the cost-effectiveness of [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET/MRI for meningioma management in a U.S. health care setting. Clinical situations in which SSTR-targeted PET is increasingly considered include differential diagnosis, assessment of tumor extent, planning for surgery or radiotherapy, distinction between recurrence and treatment-related changes, and prognostic assessment. Its use for monitoring meningioma has also been proposed. RANO plans to develop standardized PET response criteria, analogous to criteria recently established for gliomas, to support patient care and clinical trials. Evidence for radiopharmaceutical treatment of meningioma currently consists only of small case series and small, uncontrolled prospective trials. An interim analysis of an ongoing single-arm phase II trial reported that its predefined progression-free survival rate threshold at 6-mo was met and identified [68Ga]Ga-DOTATATE PET as a potentially useful imaging biomarker for evaluating treatment response. LUMEN-1; NCT06326190, the first randomized trial of [177Lu]Lu-DOTATATE for recurrent meningioma, is scheduled to begin enrollment in the first quarter of 2025. To the authors’ knowledge, it will provide the first controlled evidence for this therapy in meningioma. These developments have increased the use of SSTR-directed PET and therapy in routine care and their inclusion in clinical trials. The new EANM/ EANO/RANO/SNMMI guidelines offer expert recommendations on when to use SSTR-targeted PET, how to acquire and interpret images, and how to report findings, alongside procedure standards for SSTR-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy. They address equipment and tracer selection, patient procedures, image-analysis criteria, radiopharmaceutical dosing and administration, recommended concomitant medications, dosimetry, monitoring and follow-up schedules, prevention and management of adverse effects, and quality control. The guideline authors emphasize the need for adequately designed, controlled, prospective multicenter trials before SSTR-directed imaging and radiopharmaceutical therapy can be effectively translated into everyday neuro-oncology practice. The editorial anticipates that the guidelines will facilitate U.S. insurance reimbursement for SSTR-targeted PET in meningioma, expand access and improve outcomes, and support future efforts to obtain reimbursement for SSTR-targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy. The authors also expect this first edition of the guidelines and procedure standards to promote global harmonization and standardization, contributing to evidence-based, safe use of these approaches in people with meningioma.
